q_when.text: When do you hear the noise?

options.o1: On starting, or when trying to start
options.o2: Standing still, with the engine running
options.o3: Only while driving
options.o4: Both standing still and driving

q_start_char.text: What do you hear when you turn the key or press start?

options.o1: Clicking, the engine does not turn over
options.o2: A metallic grinding while the starter turns
options.o3: The starter spins but the engine does not catch
options.o4: A squeal or whistle right after the engine starts

options.o1: Rapid chattering, dashboard lights dim
options.o2: One clear click, then silence

q_stationary_gate.text: Does the noise appear only when you switch something on or press something — heater, A/C, clutch, steering, brake?

options.o1: Yes, it is tied to a specific action
options.o2: No, it is there on its own

q_action.text: Which action is the noise tied to?

options.o1: The heater or blower fan
options.o2: The air-conditioning button
options.o3: The clutch pedal
options.o4: The steering, brake pedal or wipers

q_hvac.text: What does it sound like with the blower on?

options.o1: Rustling or crackling that changes with fan speed
options.o2: A squeal or howl from behind the dashboard
options.o3: A series of clicks behind the dash when changing temperature or airflow
options.o4: Gurgling or trickling behind the dash

options.o2: Grinding or rumbling while the A/C runs
options.o3: A short hiss when switching on or off, and it still cools

q_clutch_idle.text: How is the noise related to the clutch pedal?

options.o1: Rustling or humming with the pedal up; it fades when you press it
options.o2: It appears or gets louder when the pedal is pressed
options.o3: Rattling or clatter at idle that changes when you press the pedal
options.o4: A creak when pressing, audible even with the engine off

q_wheel_pedal.text: What exactly is the noise tied to?

options.o1: A howl or hum when you turn the steering wheel
options.o2: Crunching or clicking when turning the wheel while parked
options.o3: A hiss from behind the dash when you press the brake pedal
options.o4: A knock or squeak in time with the wipers

options.o1: Yes, there is
options.o2: No, or I am not sure

options.o1: From above, behind the wheel arch, near the bonnet
options.o2: From the steering wheel or column, down by your feet

q_engine_cold.text: Is the noise there only on a cold engine, right after starting?

options.o1: Yes, it goes away once warm
options.o2: No, it is there when warm too

q_cold_char.text: What does the cold-engine noise sound like?

options.o1: Rapid ticking or tapping
options.o2: A dull knock that disappears once warm
options.o3: Rustling or clatter from the front of the engine
options.o4: A squeal or whistle on starting

q_tick_cold.text: Is the tapping louder outside than in the cabin, and does it smell of exhaust under the bonnet?

options.o1: Yes, louder outside and there is a smell
options.o2: No, it taps from the top of the engine, no smell

q_engine_char.text: What does the noise sound like?

options.o1: A knock or ticking
options.o2: A squeal, whistle, hum or hiss
options.o3: Ringing, rattling, popping or gurgling
options.o4: Vibration or shaking at idle

options.o1: Light, rapid ticking from the top of the engine
options.o2: A dull or sharp knock from deep inside the engine

q_tick_warm.text: Has the ticking got louder over time, or is it always the same?

options.o1: It has got louder, and is clearer when warm
options.o2: Always the same, and louder outside than in the cabin

q_knock_load.text: If you blip the throttle gently, does the knock get faster and louder?

options.o1: Yes, faster and louder
options.o2: Barely changes, or it disappears

q_squeal.text: What kind of noise is it?

options.o1: A piercing squeal or whistle
options.o2: A steady hum or rustle
options.o3: A steady hiss, like air escaping a tyre

q_hum_source.text: Where does the hum come from?

options.o1: From the front, under the bonnet, changing with engine speed
options.o2: It comes and goes by itself: in heat, in traffic, with the A/C on
options.o3: From the rear, near the tank; audible with the ignition on before starting

q_pump_check.text: Are there drips or fluid traces near the belt under the bonnet?

options.o1: Yes, drips or a smell of coolant
options.o2: It is dry
options.o3: I could not check

options.o1: A metallic rattle from under the car
options.o2: Popping or banging from the exhaust
options.o3: Gurgling or trickling behind the dashboard

options.o1: Yes, it clears quickly
options.o2: No, it is there on every stop

options.o1: A squeal or squeak
options.o2: Metal grinding on metal
options.o3: A knock or pulsing through the pedal

options.o1: A hum at speed, louder to one side
options.o2: Clicking or crunching with the wheel on full lock
options.o3: A knock when you turn the wheel
options.o4: A howl or hum when turning while parked or manoeuvring

options.o1: A knock or clunk
options.o2: A creak, like an old bed
options.o3: Rattling or clatter
options.o4: A single thud on the first move after standing a long time

options.o2: Single dull thuds over potholes and speed bumps
options.o3: The knock comes through the steering wheel, you feel it in your hands
options.o4: The clunk appeared suddenly after hitting a pothole, and one corner sits lower

options.o1: The front
options.o2: The rear
options.o3: Hard to tell

options.o2: From the cabin: dashboard, doors, trim squeaks
options.o3: From the boot, as if something is rolling around
options.o4: From the front, up near the bonnet

options.o1: It appears on or off the throttle

options.o3: It is there constantly while the car moves
options.o4: It is more of a vibration or shudder than a noise

options.o1: Metallic pinging, especially uphill
options.o2: A knock as you press or lift off the throttle
options.o3: Popping or a loud roar from the exhaust
options.o4: A howl or whistle under load

options.o3: The engine revs but the car does not accelerate; sometimes a burning smell

options.o1: A high whistle only on the throttle, gone when you lift off (turbo engine)
options.o2: A hum or whine whose pitch changes on and off the throttle at the same speed
options.o3: A monotone whine under acceleration; the gearbox is a CVT or automatic
options.o4: Louder in one gear and quieter in another; manual gearbox

q_shift_char.text: What happens when shifting or pulling away?

options.o1: A jolt or clunk shifting an automatic between D and R, or during changes
options.o2: A crunch when engaging a gear on a manual
options.o3: The car shudders as you pull away while releasing the clutch
options.o4: A single clunk underneath as you pull away or change throttle

options.o2: From 25–40 mph onwards, worse as speed rises
options.o3: In a narrow speed band, felt through the floor and body; rear- or all-wheel drive
options.o4: Only when braking, the wheel kicks back

options.o1: A steady hum or whine
options.o2: Grinding, scraping or a squeak from a wheel
options.o3: A loud roar or droning
options.o4: A whistle or moan only at high speed

options.o2: Scraping; after driving the wheel is hot and the car pulls to one side

options.o1: Yes, in the last few days
options.o2: No, not for a long time

options.o1: It stays
options.o2: It fades along with the engine speed
options.o3: I could not check

options.o1: Yes, it sounds different in different gears
options.o2: No, it depends only on engine speed

options.o1: Yes, quieter or louder to one side
options.o2: No, it is steady at any speed above 25–40 mph
options.o3: It depends on the road surface

q_hum_where.text: Is the hum from the front or the rear?

options.o1: The front
options.o2: The rear
options.o3: Hard to tell

leaf_battery.explanation: Rapid chattering when you try to start means the starter solenoid is not getting enough current: it clicks but cannot turn the engine over. Usually the battery is flat, or the terminals are corroded and loose. Dashboard lights dimming as you try confirms it.
leaf_battery.advice: Check the battery terminals: clean off any white or greenish deposit and tighten them. If that does not help, charge the battery or jump-start from another car and drive to a shop for a replacement. A battery older than four or five years is almost certainly done.

leaf_starter_solenoid.top_cause: Starter solenoid or its main contacts
leaf_starter_solenoid.explanation: One clear click with the lights staying bright means the solenoid engages but the starter motor itself does not run: burnt main contacts, worn brushes, or a stuck solenoid. Sometimes it starts on the second or third try — that is the same diagnosis.
leaf_starter_solenoid.advice: Try starting a few more times; if it only starts every other time, get to a garage within days, before you are stranded in a car park. Check and tighten the battery terminals. Tapping the starter is a way to get home once, not a fix.

leaf_starter_grind.top_cause: Starter drive gear or flywheel ring gear
leaf_starter_grind.explanation: Metallic grinding on starting means the starter pinion is not meshing properly with the flywheel ring gear: the teeth are worn or the mechanism is sticking. Every start like this eats away at both the starter and the flywheel.
leaf_starter_grind.advice: Book a garage within the week: replacing the pinion or the starter is far cheaper than the ring gear, which means dropping the gearbox. Until then, do not hold the key in the start position longer than needed, and do not retry immediately after a grind.

leaf_starter_bendix.top_cause: The starter pinion is not engaging, or ring-gear teeth are stripped
leaf_starter_bendix.explanation: If the starter spins briskly but the engine does not even try to turn, the pinion is spinning free: the one-way clutch in the starter drive is worn, or the ring-gear teeth are stripped at that spot.
leaf_starter_bendix.advice: A second attempt sometimes works, because the flywheel stops in a different position. Still, get to a garage within days: every attempt makes the damage worse. On a manual you can bump-start in an emergency — never do this with an automatic.

leaf_blower_debris.top_cause: Leaves or debris in the heater fan
alt_causes: A foreign object in the ducting
leaf_blower_debris.explanation: Rustling and crackling that changes with fan speed is almost always leaves or debris drawn through the air intake into the heater fan. It is a classic autumn problem, especially if the cabin filter is clogged or missing.
leaf_blower_debris.advice: Replace the cabin filter — the debris often sits right on it, and on many cars this is a ten-minute job you can do yourself; instructions for your model are easy to find. If the rustling remains, ask a garage to blow out and clean the fan.

leaf_blower_motor.top_cause: Heater fan motor bearing or bushings
alt_causes: The fan wheel is touching its housing
leaf_blower_motor.explanation: A squeal or howl from behind the dashboard that only appears with the blower on comes from a worn heater fan motor. The check is simple: switch the blower off and the squeal stops instantly, even with the engine running.
leaf_blower_motor.advice: It does not affect safety, but in time the motor will seize and leave you without heating — better to replace it before the cold sets in. Until then you can use the fan speeds at which the squeal is quieter.

alt_causes: Stripped teeth in the actuator gear
leaf_hvac_servo.explanation: A burst of rapid clicking or chattering behind the dash when you switch on the ignition or change the temperature is the small servo that moves the heater flaps. A short, identical burst is often just calibration. Endless chattering means the plastic gear teeth are stripped.
leaf_hvac_servo.advice: If the clicks are brief and the heating works as set, you can leave it. If the chattering drags on, or air blows somewhere other than where you set it, book a garage when convenient: it does the car no harm, but comfort suffers.

leaf_coolant_air.top_cause: Air in the cooling system (low coolant level)
leaf_coolant_air.explanation: Gurgling or trickling behind the dash is an air pocket passing through the heater matrix. Air gets into the system when the coolant level has dropped: either there is a leak somewhere or the tank cap is not holding pressure. The heater may blow warm, then cold.
leaf_coolant_air.advice: With the engine cold, check the level in the expansion tank and top it up, then watch whether it drops again. If the level keeps falling, or the heater blows cold on a hot engine, get to a garage this week. If the temperature gauge climbs or you see steam, pull over and switch the engine off.

leaf_ac_clutch.explanation: A squeal exactly at the moment the A/C engages means the clutch that connects the compressor to the belt is slipping under load. A single click on engagement is normal; a squeal points to a worn clutch or a slack belt.
leaf_ac_clutch.advice: Have it looked at within a couple of weeks: left alone, the squeal becomes constant and the compressor can seize and snap the belt. You can still use the A/C until then, but switch it off if the squeal gets worse.

alt_causes: Low oil level in the system
leaf_ac_compressor.explanation: Grinding or rumbling heard only while the A/C is running is a dying compressor or its pulley bearing. A seized compressor snaps the belt, and on many cars that belt also drives the alternator and the water pump.
leaf_ac_compressor.advice: Leave the A/C switched off for now — that will get the unit to the repair intact. Book a diagnosis within the week: while only the bearing is failing, the repair is far cheaper than replacing the compressor and flushing the whole system.

alt_causes: Normal operation of the expansion valve
leaf_ac_hiss.explanation: A brief hiss or gurgle behind the dash in the first seconds after switching the A/C on or off is refrigerant moving through the expansion valve. If the cabin still gets cold, this is the system working as intended, not a leak.
leaf_ac_hiss.advice: Nothing needs doing. The reason to check is different: if the hiss becomes constant and the cooling is weak or gone, book a diagnosis of the air-conditioning system.

leaf_gearbox_input_bearing.explanation: A rustle or hum at idle that fades when you press the clutch comes from the gearbox: with the pedal up, the input shaft turns with the engine and its worn bearing makes the noise. Press the pedal, the shaft stops and the noise goes. The belt and its pulleys do not react to the clutch pedal at all.
leaf_gearbox_input_bearing.advice: Book a diagnosis within a week or two, and be sure to mention that the noise depends on the pedal — that alone points the search in the right direction. Check the gearbox oil level. You can drive, but do not leave it for months: a failed bearing takes the shafts and gears with it.

leaf_release_bearing.explanation: A rustle or hum that appears or grows when the clutch pedal is pressed comes from the release bearing — the part that pushes on the pressure plate as you press. A worn release bearing is noisy precisely under load, that is, with the pedal down.
leaf_release_bearing.advice: Book a garage within a week or two. Keep the pedal down only when you need to — at traffic lights, use neutral and let the clutch up. A release bearing that breaks up can leave you without a clutch on the road, so do not drag this out for months.

leaf_dmf.explanation: A metallic rattle or clatter at idle from the gearbox side that changes when you press the clutch, and is loudest in the seconds while starting and switching off, is the classic signature of a worn dual-mass flywheel — the damper between engine and gearbox that absorbs shocks.
leaf_dmf.advice: Book a diagnosis within a couple of weeks and describe how the noise relates to the pedal and to starting and stopping. Replacement is not cheap, but delay ruins the clutch too and can end with the flywheel breaking up while driving. Until then, pull away gently and avoid labouring the engine at low revs.

leaf_clutch_pedal.top_cause: Clutch pedal linkage (pivot, fork or cable)
leaf_clutch_pedal.explanation: A creak when pressing the pedal that you can hear with the engine off is dry linkage: the pedal pivot, the cable or the fork. Because the noise exists without the engine running, the belt, the release bearing and the gearbox have nothing to do with it.
leaf_clutch_pedal.advice: Ask a garage to grease the pedal pivot and the fork at your next visit — this often takes minutes. There is no danger. If the pedal has also become stiff, or the clutch now bites right at the floor, have it looked at sooner.

leaf_strut_mount.explanation: Crunching or clicking when turning the wheel while parked, coming from above behind the wheel arch, is the top mount bearing — the part the top of the strut turns on as the wheel steers. Single clunks from above over potholes are a further sign.
leaf_strut_mount.advice: Book a diagnosis within a week or two: the check is simple, as a hand on the strut top under the bonnet feels the clicks straight away. You can drive, but a worn mount wears the strut faster and makes the steering return sluggish.

leaf_steering_ujoint.explanation: A click or knock you can hear and feel right in the steering wheel, down by your feet, usually comes from the universal joint on the intermediate steering shaft — the small coupling between the wheel and the rack. With the engine off, rocking the wheel left and right makes the click clearly audible.
leaf_steering_ujoint.advice: Have it checked within days: steering is a safety system and the check takes minutes. Play in the column grows over time and adds slack to the wheel.

leaf_brake_booster.top_cause: Brake servo or its vacuum hose
leaf_brake_booster.explanation: A hiss from behind the dash that appears and changes exactly as you press and release the brake pedal is air being drawn into the brake servo — the unit that reduces the effort at the pedal. The pedal usually becomes noticeably harder, and the idle may waver.
leaf_brake_booster.advice: Book a garage this week: the brakes still work without the servo, but you will have to push far harder, which is dangerous in an emergency. Check the pedal before setting off: if it has gone hard as a board, drive gently and not far.

leaf_wipers.explanation: A knock at the ends of the sweep is play in the wiper linkage joints — the mechanism that drives the arms — or loose arm nuts. An even squeak across the glass is hardened blade rubbers. The check is simple: switch the wipers off and the noise stops at once and completely.
leaf_wipers.advice: Squeaking rubbers you can replace yourself — blades are sold in any parts shop. For a knock at the ends of the sweep, have the arm nuts tightened or the linkage bushings replaced when convenient. The only safety issue here is a clear windscreen.

leaf_eps.top_cause: Electric power steering: a faint hum is normal
leaf_eps.explanation: If there is no fluid reservoir under the bonnet, the steering is electric, and a steady quiet hum when turning is it working normally, not a fault. There is simply no hydraulic pump in such a car to howl from a low fluid level.
leaf_eps.advice: The warning signs of electric steering are different: the wheel becomes heavy or stiffens in steps, crunching appears, or the steering warning light comes on. If you have any of those, get to a garage within days; if not, drive on with confidence.

leaf_exhaust_manifold.top_cause: Exhaust manifold gasket or a crack
leaf_exhaust_manifold.explanation: Rapid tapping on a cold engine that is louder outside and comes with a smell of exhaust under the bonnet is gases escaping through a burnt manifold gasket or a crack. As the metal warms it expands, the gap closes and the tapping stops.
leaf_exhaust_manifold.advice: Book a garage within a week or two: the gap grows over time, and exhaust fumes can be drawn into the cabin through the heater, which is harmful. Until it is fixed, air the cabin if you can smell exhaust.

leaf_injectors_normal.top_cause: Normal injector tick (direct injection or diesel)
leaf_injectors_normal.explanation: On direct-injection engines (TSI, GDI and the like) and on diesels, the injectors and the high-pressure pump always tick — that is how they work. The giveaways: the sound is the same cold and hot, louder outside than in the cabin, and it does not depend on how old the oil is.
leaf_injectors_normal.advice: Nothing needs doing. What should concern you is different: if the ticking has become noticeably louder than before, changed once warm, or arrived together with a loss of power — then book a diagnosis.

leaf_vacuum_leak.top_cause: Air leak (vacuum hose or intake gasket)
leaf_vacuum_leak.explanation: A steady hiss under the bonnet, like air from a punctured tyre, is unmetered air being drawn in through a cracked hose or an intake gasket. The engine often runs unevenly because of it: the idle wanders and the check-engine light may come on.
leaf_vacuum_leak.advice: Book a diagnosis within days, especially if the idle wanders: tracing an air leak is a standard job. You can look yourself at the thin rubber hoses under the bonnet for cracks, without removing anything.

leaf_cooling_fan.top_cause: Radiator cooling fan (bushings, or running constantly)
leaf_cooling_fan.explanation: A hum or roar that switches itself on and off — in the heat, in traffic, with the A/C on — is the radiator cooling fan. A noisy fan means either worn motor bushings or that it runs constantly because of a sensor or the thermostat. Running on for a couple of minutes after switching off is normal.
leaf_cooling_fan.advice: If the fan roars constantly from start-up on a cold engine, book a diagnosis within days: the cooling system is not working properly. Watch the temperature gauge; if it climbs, pull over and switch the engine off.

leaf_fuel_pump.explanation: A steady buzz or whine from the rear, under the back seat or near the tank, is the fuel pump. Hearing it for a couple of seconds when you switch on the ignition is normal, but a loud whine you notice while driving points to a worn pump or a clogged filter making it strain.
leaf_fuel_pump.advice: Book a fuel pressure check within a week or two. Do not drive for long on the low-fuel light: at the bottom of the tank the pump cools less well and wears faster. If the car has started hesitating under load or is hard to start, go sooner.

leaf_catalyst.explanation: A ringing rattle or shuffling from under the car nearer the engine, which grows when you blip the throttle and comes with a loss of power or a changed exhaust smell, is the ceramic inside the converter breaking apart. The fragments rattle in the casing, and the blocked honeycomb chokes the engine.
leaf_catalyst.advice: Book a diagnosis within days: fragments of ceramic can be drawn into the engine, and that is an expensive repair. A simple check at a garage is a light tap on the converter body once cold — you can hear the loose pieces inside. This is not one to put off.

leaf_at_jerk.top_cause: Automatic gearbox: old fluid, wear, or play in the driveline
leaf_at_jerk.explanation: A jolt or clunk exactly as you move the selector between D and R, or during gear changes, points to wear or old fluid in the automatic: the gear engages with a shock, and play in the driveline amplifies it. Sagging mounts clunk in a similar way, so the diagnosis is worth confirming.
leaf_at_jerk.advice: First check the level and condition of the gearbox fluid — dark, with a burnt smell, means it needs changing, and in many cases that is enough. Book a diagnosis within a week or two and say exactly which changes jolt. Until then, move the selector only at a full stop with the brake pressed.

leaf_synchro.top_cause: Gearbox synchronisers, or the clutch not fully disengaging
leaf_synchro.explanation: A crunch as you engage a gear on a manual means the gears meet at different speeds. If only one or two gears crunch — usually second or third — their synchronisers are worn; if every gear crunches, the clutch is not fully disengaging and the gearbox never lets go.
leaf_synchro.advice: Check the clutch pedal free play and the gearbox oil level — a garage will start there too. Book a diagnosis within a couple of weeks. Until then shift more slowly, with a pause in neutral: it crunches less and wears less.

leaf_clutch_judder.explanation: Shuddering strictly while you release the clutch pulling away, with the car driving smoothly once fully engaged, means the clutch is grabbing in steps: the disc is worn, contaminated with oil, or the pressure plate is distorted. Engine mounts shake at idle as well, whereas this lives only in the pull-away phase.
leaf_clutch_judder.advice: Book a diagnosis within a week or two: judder does not go away on its own and usually gets worse. Until then pull away gently, with slightly more revs, and do not slip the clutch. If you smell burning, the clutch is on its way out — do not delay the visit.

leaf_driveline_lash.top_cause: Driveshaft universal joints or play in the driveline
leaf_driveline_lash.explanation: A single clunk or click from under the middle or rear of the car as you pull away and on and off the throttle is slack in the drive path: most often worn universal joints on the propshaft (rear- and all-wheel drive) or loose subframe mountings.
leaf_driveline_lash.advice: Book a diagnosis within a week or two: on a lift, play in the propshaft is found by hand in a minute. Do not put it off — a worn universal joint can break up at speed. Until then pull away and lift off more gently.

leaf_clutch_slip.explanation: If the revs rise and the engine roars on the throttle while the car barely accelerates, the clutch is slipping and not transmitting drive: the disc is worn or contaminated with oil. It shows most uphill and in the higher gears, often with an acrid burning smell. A worn automatic slips in the same way.
leaf_clutch_slip.advice: Get to a garage this week: a slipping clutch slips until there is no drive at all, usually at the least convenient moment. Until then drive gently, no overtaking and no towing, and change down before a hill. If the burning smell gets stronger, do not delay another day.

leaf_turbo.explanation: A light, even turbo whistle under load is normal on a turbo engine. What should concern you is change: the whistle grew louder or changed pitch, a howl appeared, or the car lost power. That is either air escaping from the boost pipework or wear in the turbo shaft bearing.
leaf_turbo.advice: If the pitch has changed or power has dropped, book a diagnosis within days: a leaking hose is a cheap fix, while neglected turbo wear ends in replacement. Keep an eye on oil consumption. Until it is checked, avoid running the engine to the limiter and let the turbo cool for a minute or two at idle after hard driving.

alt_causes: Low oil level in the differential
leaf_final_drive.explanation: A whine or hum that changes pitch on and off the throttle at the same road speed — louder under power, quieter coasting, or the other way round — is the signature of worn final drive gears, the pair that sends drive to the wheels. A wheel bearing, by contrast, does not react to the throttle at all.
leaf_final_drive.advice: Check the oil level in the differential and book a diagnosis within the week: caught early, fresh oil and an adjustment are often enough; left late, the gear set needs replacing. Postpone long motorway trips until it is checked.

leaf_cvt_whine.top_cause: CVT or automatic gearbox (bearings, belt, torque converter)
leaf_cvt_whine.explanation: A monotone metallic whine under acceleration on a car with a CVT or automatic, which follows the throttle rather than road speed, is usually the pulley bearings in a CVT or the pump in an automatic. A CVT is especially sensitive to the age of its fluid.
leaf_cvt_whine.advice: Start with the level and condition of the gearbox fluid — that is half of these cases. Book a diagnosis within the week and drive gently until then, with no hard acceleration and no towing. Repairing a CVT early costs many times less than repairing it late.

leaf_gearbox_whine.explanation: A whine whose loudness depends on the gear you are in — loud in one, quieter in another, gone in neutral while coasting — comes from the manual gearbox: worn shaft bearings or one particular pair of gears. A wheel bearing hums the same in every gear.
leaf_gearbox_whine.advice: Check the gearbox oil level — a drop is a common cause in itself. Book a diagnosis within a week or two and say in which gears it is loudest: that narrows the search. You can drive, but do not let a growing whine run on.
